course.title: Instants, offsets and zones
course.description: Moments versus wall clocks in java.time — epoch milliseconds, signed Durations, LocalDateTime needing an offset, same-instant versus same-local zone changes, the spring-forward day (Period versus Duration), truncation into time buckets, timeline ordering across zones, and the midnight fencepost between millis and dates. Fixed historic timestamps only; region zones appear once, on a 2021 date whose tz history is immutable. Complements javabootcamp's date drills (LocalDate arithmetic, strict parsing, injected Clock, month-end clamping, DST debugging hunt).

javadrills/09-instants-and-zones/01-epoc.instructions:
**Skills:** Instant · epoch millis  
**Level:** ★☆☆

**Interview prompt.** "The event log stores timestamps as epoch milliseconds; the API speaks ISO-8601. Convert both ways."

**Why it works.** An `Instant` is a point on the UTC timeline, stored as a count since the epoch `1970-01-01T00:00:00Z`. `Instant.parse` reads the ISO-8601 form ending in `Z`, `toEpochMilli()` gives the millisecond count, and `Instant.ofEpochMilli` goes back. No time zone is involved anywhere — that is what makes an instant unambiguous. Moments before 1970 simply have negative counts.

**Your task.** Implement two methods:
- `toMillis(String iso)` → the epoch milliseconds of an ISO-8601 instant such as `"2024-01-15T10:30:00Z"`.
- `fromMillis(long ms)` → the `Instant` at that many milliseconds since the epoch.

**Worked example.** `toMillis("2024-01-15T10:30:00Z")` returns **1705314600000**.
javadrills/09-instants-and-zones/01-epoc.explanation:
An instant is a millisecond count since the epoch.

For `"2024-01-15T10:30:00Z"`:
- 2024-01-15 is epoch day 19737 (54 years of 365 days plus 13 leap days to 2024-01-01 = 19723, plus 14)
- `19737 × 86400 = 1705276800` seconds at midnight, plus 10:30 = 37800 s → 1705314600 s
- times 1000 → **1705314600000** ms, and `Instant.ofEpochMilli` maps it straight back

Kinship: javabootcamp's date drills work with `LocalDate` and an injected `Clock` but never touch `Instant` conversions; this is unowned. In an interview, "store instants (UTC millis), render in zones at the edge" is the architecture rule this supports.
hints: No time zone is needed — the trailing Z already says UTC.
Instant.parse reads ISO-8601, Instant.toEpochMilli and Instant.ofEpochMilli convert to and from milliseconds.
an instant is just the millisecond count since the epoch wearing an ISO costume — parse and convert in either direction

javadrills/09-instants-and-zones/02-dura.instructions:
**Skills:** Duration  
**Level:** ★★☆

**Interview prompt.** "A ticket opened at 10:00 has a 30-minute SLA. Report the seconds left — and when it is breached, by how much."

**Why it works.** `Duration.between(a, b)` is the elapsed time from `a` to `b`, and it is SIGNED: if `b` is earlier than `a`, the duration is negative. That sign is useful, not an error — "seconds left until the deadline" turns negative exactly when the deadline has passed, and its magnitude is the breach. `toMinutes()` and `toSeconds()` read the duration in whole units.

**Your task.** Implement two methods:
- `minutesBetween(Instant a, Instant b)` → whole minutes from `a` to `b` (negative when `b` is earlier).
- `slaSecondsLeft(Instant opened, int slaMinutes, Instant now)` → seconds from `now` until `opened + slaMinutes`; negative when the SLA is breached.

**Worked example.** `minutesBetween(10:00Z, 11:30Z)` on the same day is **90**, and reversed it is **-90**.
javadrills/09-instants-and-zones/02-dura.explanation:
`Duration.between` keeps its sign.

For `slaSecondsLeft(10:00:00Z, 30, 10:31:00Z)`:
- the deadline is `10:00:00Z + 30 min = 10:30:00Z`
- `Duration.between(10:31:00Z, 10:30:00Z)` runs backwards by one minute → `-60` seconds
- the negative answer IS the breach: 60 seconds late; at `10:29:30Z` the same formula gives **30** seconds left

Kinship: javabootcamp 10/07 does deadline and budget math on raw longs; this drill is the `Duration` API itself and its sign. In an interview, "don't take abs() — the sign tells you which side of the deadline you are on" is the detail that matters.
hints: Try swapping the two arguments and see what the result does.
Duration.between returns a negative Duration when the end is before the start; Instant.plus with Duration.ofMinutes builds the deadline.
Duration between keeps its sign so a negative answer is the breach measured in the same units

javadrills/09-instants-and-zones/03-wall.instructions:
**Skills:** LocalDateTime · ZoneOffset  
**Level:** ★★☆

**Interview prompt.** "The meeting is stored as `2024-06-01T09:00` — no zone. Is that one moment? Show me two moments it could be."

**Why it works.** A `LocalDateTime` is a wall-clock reading — a date and a time with NO zone or offset — so it does not identify a moment. Attaching an offset with `toInstant(ZoneOffset)` pins it to the timeline: 09:00 at `+00:00` is `09:00Z`, while 09:00 at `+02:00` is `07:00Z`. The same wall time at two offsets is two moments exactly the offset difference apart.

**Your task.** Implement two methods:
- `toInstant(LocalDateTime wall, ZoneOffset off)` → the moment that `wall` denotes at offset `off`.
- `gapSeconds(LocalDateTime wall, ZoneOffset a, ZoneOffset b)` → how many seconds apart (non-negative) the moments `wall@a` and `wall@b` are.

**Worked example.** For `2024-06-01T09:00`, `gapSeconds(wall, +00:00, +02:00)` is **7200**.
javadrills/09-instants-and-zones/03-wall.explanation:
A wall time becomes a moment only with an offset.

For `2024-06-01T09:00` at `+00:00` and `+02:00`:
- at `+00:00` the moment is `09:00Z`
- at `+02:00` the clocks run two hours ahead of UTC, so 09:00 there is `07:00Z`
- the two moments are `9 − 7 = 2` hours apart → **7200** seconds

Kinship: javabootcamp's date drills stay inside `LocalDate`; the "LocalDateTime is zone-naive" interview staple is unowned there. In an interview, "a LocalDateTime is not a timestamp — store an Instant or an OffsetDateTime" is the fix.
hints: Ask what instant 09:00 is when you do not know which city's clock says it.
LocalDateTime.toInstant takes a ZoneOffset; Duration.between measures the gap and Math.abs drops its direction.
a local date-time only becomes a moment once an offset is attached and two different offsets yield moments a full offset apart

javadrills/09-instants-and-zones/04-same.instructions:
**Skills:** ZonedDateTime · zone conversion  
**Level:** ★★★

**Interview prompt.** "A 17:00 meeting at `+01:00`. One colleague wants to see it on their `+09:00` calendar; another wants to 'move the meeting to Tokyo'. Which java.time call does each one need?"

**Why it works.** `ZonedDateTime` has two ways to change zone. `withZoneSameInstant(z)` keeps the MOMENT and repaints the clock face for the new zone — the viewer's calendar: 17:00 at `+01:00` is 16:00Z, which is 01:00 the next day at `+09:00`. `withZoneSameLocal(z)` keeps the CLOCK FACE (17:00) and attaches the new zone — that is a different moment, here 8 hours earlier. Mixing them up silently moves meetings.

**Your task.** Implement two methods:
- `asSeenIn(ZonedDateTime meeting, ZoneId viewer)` → the same moment shown in the viewer's zone.
- `movedTo(ZonedDateTime meeting, ZoneId newZone)` → the same wall-clock time in the new zone.

**Worked example.** For a meeting at `2024-03-10T17:00+01:00`, `asSeenIn(meeting, ZoneId.of("+09:00"))` shows hour **1** on March 11.
javadrills/09-instants-and-zones/04-same.explanation:
Same instant repaints the clock; same local repaints the moment.

For `2024-03-10T17:00+01:00`:
- the moment is `16:00Z`
- `withZoneSameInstant(+09:00)`: `16:00Z + 9h` = **01:00 on March 11** at `+09:00` — same moment
- `withZoneSameLocal(+09:00)`: 17:00 at `+09:00` = `08:00Z`, which is `16:00 − 08:00` = 8 h = **28800** s earlier than the original

Kinship: javabootcamp's date drills never convert between zones; this pair of calls is unowned. In an interview, "display uses same-instant; rescheduling uses same-local — and then you must tell the attendees" is the distinction.
hints: Decide whether the moment or the clock face must survive the change.
ZonedDateTime.withZoneSameInstant keeps the instant; ZonedDateTime.withZoneSameLocal keeps the local date-time.
same-instant repaints the clock face for a new wall while same-local keeps the face and quietly picks a different moment

javadrills/09-instants-and-zones/05-dst-.instructions:
**Skills:** DST · Period vs Duration  
**Level:** ★★★

**Interview prompt.** "A job runs at noon Paris time every day. On the night clocks spring forward, is 'tomorrow at noon' 24 hours away? Show me with java.time."

**Why it works.** On 2021-03-28 the `Europe/Paris` zone jumped from 02:00 to 03:00 (CET `+01:00` → CEST `+02:00`) — this is fixed historical tz data, so the result never changes. `plusDays(1)` adds a calendar day: it keeps the WALL CLOCK (12:00) and lets the elapsed time shrink to 23 hours. `plus(Duration.ofHours(24))` adds exactly 24 hours of ELAPSED time and lets the wall clock drift to 13:00. On an ordinary day the two agree.

**Your task.** Implement three methods (`z` is a `ZonedDateTime` in a region zone):
- `tomorrowSameWall(ZonedDateTime z)` → the same wall time on the next calendar day.
- `in24Hours(ZonedDateTime z)` → exactly 24 elapsed hours later.
- `realHoursUntilTomorrow(ZonedDateTime z)` → the elapsed hours from `z` to `tomorrowSameWall(z)`.

**Worked example.** For `z = 2021-03-27T12:00` in `Europe/Paris`, `realHoursUntilTomorrow(z)` is **23** — the spring-forward day is 23 hours long.
javadrills/09-instants-and-zones/05-dst-.explanation:
A calendar day is not always 24 hours.

For `z = 2021-03-27T12:00+01:00[Europe/Paris]` (= `11:00Z`):
- `plusDays(1)` → `2021-03-28T12:00+02:00` (= `10:00Z`): the wall clock stays at 12:00, the offset moved to `+02:00`
- elapsed time `11:00Z → 10:00Z next day` is **23** hours
- `plus(Duration.ofHours(24))` → `2021-03-28T11:00Z` = **13:00** `+02:00` — same input, different API, different answer

Kinship: javabootcamp 19/08 is a DST debugging HUNT; this drill states the Period-vs-Duration arithmetic rule and drills it directly. In an interview, "schedule in calendar units for humans, measure in durations for machines" is the rule to state.
hints: Compare what a person means by tomorrow at noon with what a stopwatch means by 24 hours.
ZonedDateTime.plusDays keeps the local time and adjusts the offset; ZonedDateTime.plus with Duration.ofHours adds elapsed time; Duration.between measures elapsed time.
plus days keeps the wall clock and lets the day shrink while plus a duration keeps real elapsed time and lets the wall clock drift

javadrills/09-instants-and-zones/06-trun.instructions:
**Skills:** Instant · truncation  
**Level:** ★★☆

**Interview prompt.** "Group request timestamps into hourly buckets for a chart, and give me a per-minute key for a fixed-window rate limiter."

**Why it works.** `Instant.truncatedTo(ChronoUnit.HOURS)` drops everything below the hour: `10:47:33.250Z` becomes `10:00:00Z`, which is exactly the start of its bucket — every instant in the same hour truncates to the same value, and an instant already on the hour is unchanged. For a numeric minute key, truncate to minutes and divide the epoch seconds by 60: all instants in one minute share a key, and the next minute's key is one larger.

**Your task.** Implement two methods:
- `hourBucket(Instant t)` → the start of `t`'s hour.
- `minuteKey(Instant t)` → `t` truncated to the minute, as epoch seconds divided by 60.

**Worked example.** `hourBucket(Instant.parse("2024-01-15T10:47:33.250Z"))` is `2024-01-15T10:00:00Z`.
javadrills/09-instants-and-zones/06-trun.explanation:
Truncation maps every instant to the start of its bucket.

For `minuteKey(2024-01-15T10:47:33.250Z)`:
- truncating to minutes gives `10:47:00Z`
- 2024-01-15 midnight is 1705276800 s = 28421280 minutes; plus 10 h (600 min) and 47 min → **28421927**
- `10:48:00Z` is the next minute → 28421928; `hourBucket` of the same instant is `10:00:00Z`

Kinship: javabootcamp 10/02 builds fixed-window counters with raw millisecond division; this drill is the time-API idiom for the same bucketing. In an interview, mention that truncation is UTC-based — for hourly buckets in a local zone with a half-hour offset you must truncate a ZonedDateTime instead.
hints: A bucket key is the instant with its smaller units thrown away.
Instant.truncatedTo takes a ChronoUnit such as HOURS or MINUTES; Instant.getEpochSecond gives whole seconds since the epoch.
truncatedTo chops the instant down to the start of its unit which is exactly the bucket key a fixed window needs

javadrills/09-instants-and-zones/07-comp.instructions:
**Skills:** ZonedDateTime · ordering  
**Level:** ★★☆

**Interview prompt.** "Two log lines: `10:00+09:00` and `09:00+01:00`. Which happened first? And are `17:00+01:00` and `01:00+09:00` (next day) the same moment — are they `equals`?"

**Why it works.** To order moments, compare them on the TIMELINE: `10:00+09:00` is `01:00Z` and `09:00+01:00` is `08:00Z`, so the one whose wall clock reads LATER happened first. Compare by `toInstant()` (or `ChronoZonedDateTime.timeLineOrder()`). For equality there are two questions: `isEqual` asks "same instant?" and is true across zones, while `equals` also demands the same local date-time and zone, so it is false for the same moment seen from two zones.

**Your task.** Implement three methods:
- `earliest(List<ZonedDateTime> zs)` → the element at the earliest instant (the list is non-empty).
- `sameMoment(ZonedDateTime a, ZonedDateTime b)` → whether they are the same instant.
- `looksIdentical(ZonedDateTime a, ZonedDateTime b)` → whether they are `equals` (same instant, same wall time, same zone).

**Worked example.** `earliest` of `2024-03-10T09:00+01:00` and `2024-03-10T10:00+09:00` is the `10:00+09:00` one — it is `01:00Z`.
javadrills/09-instants-and-zones/07-comp.explanation:
Order and compare moments on the timeline, not on the wall.

For `09:00+01:00` versus `10:00+09:00` on 2024-03-10:
- `09:00+01:00` is `08:00Z`; `10:00+09:00` is `01:00Z`
- `01:00Z` is earlier → `earliest` returns the `10:00+09:00` value even though its wall clock reads later
- `17:00+01:00` and `01:00+09:00` the next day are both `16:00Z`: `isEqual` is true, `equals` is false (different local time and zone)

Kinship: javabootcamp's date drills compare `LocalDate`s only; ordering and equality across zones is unowned. In an interview, "use isEqual/isBefore for moments — equals is for value identity" is the precise answer.
hints: Convert each value to UTC in your head before deciding which came first.
Comparator.comparing with ZonedDateTime::toInstant orders by the timeline; ZonedDateTime.isEqual compares instants; equals compares local date-time, offset and zone.
order moments on the timeline not on the wall — isEqual compares instants while equals also demands the same zone

javadrills/09-instants-and-zones/08-epoc.instructions:
**Skills:** LocalDate · epoch millis  
**Level:** ★★☆

**Interview prompt.** "A report groups events by UTC date from epoch millis. Prove that the last millisecond of a day stays on that day, and compute where a day starts at a given offset."

**Why it works.** A date only exists relative to an offset: `Instant.ofEpochMilli(ms).atOffset(ZoneOffset.UTC).toLocalDate()` reads the UTC calendar date of a moment. Days are half-open `[midnight, next midnight)`, so `23:59:59.999` belongs to its day and one millisecond later is the next day — the fencepost. In the other direction, `date.atStartOfDay(offset)` is that date's midnight at the offset; for `+02:00` that midnight happens two hours EARLIER on the UTC timeline than UTC midnight.

**Your task.** Implement two methods:
- `utcDateOf(long ms)` → the UTC calendar date containing the epoch millisecond `ms`.
- `startOfDayMillis(LocalDate d, ZoneOffset off)` → the epoch milliseconds of midnight starting `d` at offset `off`.

**Worked example.** `utcDateOf(1705363199999L)` (`2024-01-15T23:59:59.999Z`) is `2024-01-15`, while `utcDateOf(1705363200000L)` is `2024-01-16`.
javadrills/09-instants-and-zones/08-epoc.explanation:
Days are half-open intervals on a chosen offset.

For `utcDateOf(1705363199999L)` and `utcDateOf(1705363200000L)`:
- 2024-01-16 is epoch day 19738, and `19738 × 86400000 = 1705363200000` — the first millisecond of the 16th
- `1705363199999` is one millisecond before that → `2024-01-15T23:59:59.999Z` → **2024-01-15**
- `1705363200000` → **2024-01-16**; and midnight of the 15th at `+02:00` is `1705276800000 − 7200000 = 1705269600000`

Kinship: javabootcamp 04/05 does `LocalDate` arithmetic; this drill is the conversion fencepost between epoch millis and dates. In an interview, "a date range is `[start, nextStart)` — never `<= 23:59:59`" is the rule that avoids losing the last second.
hints: Name the offset first — a millisecond count has no date until you pick one.
Instant.atOffset gives an OffsetDateTime whose toLocalDate is the calendar date; LocalDate.atStartOfDay accepts a ZoneOffset because it is a ZoneId.
the last millisecond of a day and the first of the next differ by one — convert through an explicit offset and the fencepost lands exactly at midnight
